properties.text:
EV-16 (asc-9an) -- how large can `asc types brief` get before a model stops acting on it, and does the hook raise the recording rate? PARTIAL: Q1 measured and decided, Q2/Q3 NOT MEASURED. Full record: docs/evidence/EV-16.md, pre-registered under sha256 a919cfd604acfc7619d839dcc8d32d3f9cc98db5b36f68093eb811ae69655a12.

QUESTION: four parts -- (1) the brief's cost as the registry grows, (2) the size at which a model stops acting on it, (3) whether the hook raises the recording rate over no brief and over a manually pulled brief, (4) the cap asc doctor should enforce.

METHOD: `asc types brief` driven through the real binary over registries of N active types for N in {4, 9, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400}, output tokenized with gpt-tokenizer (o200k) and @anthropic-ai/tokenizer. N=4 is the real shipped starter set and N=9 the real frozen EV-11 store; larger N extends the real starter prose under distinct names. The model arms were pre-registered as four real claude -p sessions and were NOT run -- see below.

MEASUREMENT: bytes = 301.19*N + 6.7, r2 = 0.999999 -- exactly linear, no truncation, no fixed overhead. 4 types = 1,189 bytes / 262 tokens; 9 = 1,655 / 369; 100 = 30,109 / 6,742; 400 = 120,484 / 26,992. TWO DESIGN ASSUMPTIONS OVERTURNED. (a) The benchmark this task was written against is stale by 9x: `bd prime` measures 45,639 bytes today, not the 4.9 KB stated in TASKS.md and ARCHITECTURE.md:277, and this repo's own tool-results/ holds 70 persisted SessionStart hook outputs ranging 10,576 to 44,645 bytes and growing monotonically with the tracker. (b) The brief tokenizes at ~4.5 code points/token, stable across the range, so budgeting it with ascend's own CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 2 (calibrated in EV-13 on JSON output) over-estimates it by 2.2x and would fire a cap at ~13 types instead of ~30.

DECISION: a 2,000-token COST cap on `asc types brief`, enforced by asc doctor (asc-12a) -- ~30 types at real starter prose, ~50 at the denser ingested prose, about a fifth of what bd prime costs today, ~1% of a 200k window. Expressed in tokens, not type count, because a count is a proxy whose exchange rate swings 1.6x with how long authors write record_when (measured 183.9 bytes/type ingested vs 301.2 in the starter set). The check must use the brief's own measured ratio, not CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 2. This is a COST cap and asc doctor should say so in its own output; the COMPLIANCE cap stays unset.

CONFIDENCE: high for the cost curve (seven points over a 100x range, two independent tokenizers agreeing within 4%, and the two real registries fall on the same line as the constructed ones). High for bd prime's 45,639 bytes and that it grows. Medium for the 4.5 ratio -- neither tokenizer is Claude's. LOW FOR EVERYTHING BEHAVIOURAL, and that is the honest headline: the bead's own question -- does the hook raise the recording rate -- HAS NO ANSWER HERE. asc-1q9 proved the hook FIRES and injects; nothing has proved the injection changes what gets recorded, and no green gate in this repo distinguishes the two. empirical-planning P5 records the same failure from this user's own align build: given an open-ended task the agent made ZERO calls to the new tool. Availability is not adoption.

WHY Q2/Q3 DID NOT RUN: the first harness used --dangerously-skip-permissions and the auto-mode classifier correctly refused it -- the user had authorized scoping, not running agents with approvals off. Rewritten to what the denial suggested (explicit --allowedTools + --permission-mode dontAsk, no bypass flag), the classifier then returned its model-unavailable timeout on every attempt including a trivial probe. Deferred to asc-4so.2, which needs an Anthropic-account session the user will drive. The three-arm design and its five predictions are pre-registered in EV-16 and survive intact for whoever runs it.

KNOWN GAPS: the arms for N>9 hold per-type prose length at the starter mean, so the curve is cost against COUNT and not against prose novelty; n=2 for real registries, which is the generalization floor and not above it; and bd prime's 70 archived outputs are one tracker's growth curve.

asc-4so.1 measurement, driven rather than argued. The brief is name + record_when only (brief.ts:27-31), confirmed by running it. Swept the four starter types' property descriptions for verbatim-demanding language: exactly one hit, stuck_event.error_text, confirming the bead's n=1 scope. Cost of the fix, measured through the real binary with two tokenizers: 1189 -> 1353 bytes, 262 -> 299 anthropic tokens, +37. That is 14.9% of asc-9an's 2000-token cap. Proven to ship: a project carrying the old prose returns outcome=prose-updated on re-init and receives the clause. Four mutations, all fired, all restores byte-identical. The one that removes the clause breaks the assertion naming it; the one that strips error_text's verbatim wording makes the scan find nothing and the negative control fails loudly rather than going vacuously green. UNVALIDATED AND NOT TO BE OVERSTATED: whether a model told to preserve raw output actually does so. No model was run against this prose.

evidence_text: EV-17 (asc-nai), measured 2026-09-15. Question: of searches that return rows, how many are silent about text the corpus holds? Corpus earned from 859 real transcripts via asc ingest claude-code: 1,574 entries, 1.3% carrying evidence_text (20 of 1,574) -- identical to EV-15's backfilled 20 of 1,491, refuting EV-15's prediction that live workflows would set it far more often. Bound: 4 of 5 types have indexed == 0, so rows == 0 unconditionally and the assist always fires; the silent case is confined to user_correction. Rate, exhaustive over all 102 distinct property terms in that type: 95 visible, 7 SILENT, 0 plain -- 6.86% of all searches, 100.00% of searches that returned rows, with zero plain cases. Sharpest illustration: asc search user_correction bash returns a correction that merely quotes the word while withholding the correction whose tool_name IS Bash, and the same term against tool_denial names tool_name=Bash across 446 entries -- the type that indexes nothing says more than the type that indexes and holds the term. The bead's constructed two-entry stuck_event case reproduced verbatim through the real CLI. P1, P4, P5 confirmed; P2 confirmed and exceeded; P3 refuted as operationalized (the driver is prose overlap, not term commonness -- session_id supplies 50 of 102 terms and yields zero silent cases). Cost of closing it: 0.1228 ms, under the pre-registered 1 ms threshold but 1.01x the FTS search itself. Disposition: the pre-registered under-1% exit does NOT apply; confirmed a real defect, one type wide and total within it. Remedy left to the user because it changes the versioned --json output contract.

asc-nai closed, commit ac2bf4e. asc search now reports property-value matches on every search, not only on a zero result. Verified by re-running the identical 102-term query set against the fixed binary: rows==0 unchanged at 95, rows>0 unchanged at 7 (the fix does not touch the FTS half), and UNREPORTED -- rows returned with no reported value holding the term -- goes from 7 of 7 to 0 of 7. Four mutations of the pre-fix behaviour all fire. OUTPUT_CONTRACT_VERSION 1 -> 2, now pinned in exactly one test so a bump is one deliberate edit. Not claimed: that a caller reaches the term -- reported is not adopted.

asc-i6z closed, commit d5c84f7. Two false-green test gaps closed, no behaviour change: the doubled-warning-prefix guard now asserts a Warning: is rendered and that exactly one warning: appears in the line (counted case-insensitively, because import renders the source path between the prefix and the message and the doubled line there is 'Warning: <path>: warning:'); and the missing-operand test now pipes a real document and asserts the discriminator -- 'Missing 1 required arg', no ENOENT, nothing registered -- rather than an exit code the defective path also produces. The define half of the piped-value block had become an exact duplicate and was folded into it; test count 1212 -> 1211, the one removed being a test that could not fail. Five mutations, all five fire, sources restore byte-identical. Gates green.

properties.text: The 8pp-truncation fixture measures a real error message's size, and asc-98c moved it: the arms carried 75,441 bytes before and 70,154 after, and the 2,000-property variant 628,078 before and 588,075 after. The difference is the gutter -- a marker and three spaces of indent on every continuation line, of which a 240-property refusal has thousands. The file's conclusion (guard absent and guard present deliver identical bytes) is an equality between two arms, which a change to how a line is rendered moves together, so the 24-run study was cited rather than repeated and the two counts were re-measured against the built binary directly. The write was re-instrumented too, because asc-98c moved it from oclif's console.error to emitStderr's process.stderr.write: still one large write, still returning true with writableLength 0, which is the property that docblock's open question rests on.

EV-18 (asc-9y1) -- what does one `asc record` call cost the agent that makes it? MEASURED for the estimator arm and the floor; the realized arm is NOT MEASURED. Full record: docs/evidence/EV-18.md, pre-registered under sha256 cafed1f4346f560404cbb2c48a6dc9107d33058e1c78a1c118aea2e7a4823d72.

QUESTION: five parts, named before running -- (1) wall-clock p50/p95 over 20 real recordings, the number EV-8 deliberately did not measure; (2) context tokens per call on both shipped surfaces; (3) realized cost in a live session against estimateTokens; (4) whether a recording runs to completion under an allowlist grant WITHOUT a permission prompt; (5) which surface wins and by how much, since the bead's decision rule presumes there is one surface to simplify.

METHOD: two arms, pre-registered. Arm A: 20 real entries -- the property sets already in this repo's own dogfood store, not authored for the experiment -- recorded through the real binary on both shipped surfaces (S1 flags, S2 document-on-stdin), each timed from spawn to exit with the exit code recorded so a failed call cannot be averaged in as a fast one. Plus a floor measurement, four rungs at the same n=20. Arm B: a bounded headless session granted exactly Bash(asc record:*) under --permission-mode dontAsk, no bypass flag -- written, dry-run verified, NOT RUN.

MEASUREMENT: THE BEAD'S PREMISE IS FALSIFIED. S1 mean 794.15 tokens, S2 mean 795.25 -- a difference of 0.14%, with every paired per-entry delta between -7 and +7 tokens. The cost is not the surface: per call the entry is 1386 chars (87.17%), the surface 21 chars (1.32%), the output 183 chars (11.51%). S1's ENTIRE surface -- every --prop=, every property name, every quote -- is 19 characters per call. So the decision rule ('if a record costs more than a few hundred tokens, simplify the surface') FIRED at 2.65x its pre-registered 300-token threshold, and the action it prescribes cannot reach the number that fired it: a zero-cost surface still leaves 698 tokens per call, 2.3x over. The rule presumes a fat surface over thin content; the measurement finds the reverse, by a factor of 66. WALL-CLOCK: p50 173.894 ms, not the predicted <100 ms, and the floor says why that was never reachable -- bare `node -e 0` 52.770 ms, `asc --version` 147.820, `asc query` 157.068, `asc record` 173.894. Oclif dispatch costs 95.050 ms before any ascend code runs, and the recording itself (open the store, validate, insert 18 columns, update the expression indexes, commit) is 16.826 ms = 9.7% of the call. EV-8's 'everything else is process start' now has its number: 88%. A SECOND FINDING the bead did not ask for: cli-best-practices, which this project adopted, sets the target '<100 ms to --help'; `asc --help` measures 171.414 ms p50 / 242.150 ms p95 -- 71% over at p50, and the slowest of the four rungs, above `asc query`, which does strictly more work. It needs its own bead and is not fixed here.

DECISION: do not simplify the surface. The rule fired and is NOT being re-scoped -- its PREMISE is recorded as overturned, per KICKOFF.md ('if the design and the evidence disagree, the evidence wins -- record what it overturned'). There is no cheap fallback: the content is the answer to 'what did the agent learn', which is what ascend exists to store, and the only ways to lower 1386 chars/call are to record less or to record less often -- product decisions about the deferred-analysis premise, not surface decisions, and not this task's to make.

CONFIDENCE: high that the two surfaces cost the same -- 20 paired calls each, every delta inside the noise band, and both surfaces independently carrying 1386 identical chars/call of content, which is the cross-check. High on the decomposition, which is char counting on the exact bytes each surface carried rather than a model. High on the floor -- four rungs, n=20 each, 0 failures, with an internally consistent ordering. MEDIUM on the token figures, in the direction that does not matter: estimateTokens is a calibrated constant that runs 9-28% high, so 794 is an upper estimate, and this cannot change any conclusion here -- the surface share is a ratio of character counts, so a uniformly 25%-high estimator leaves 1.32% at 1.32%, while the threshold is crossed at 2.65x. LOW on anything about a real session's cost: arm B did not run, and no number in this record is a realized one.

ARM B NOT RUN, AND WHY: ten launch attempts, foreground and background, every one refused before execution with 'deepseek-v4.1-flash:cloud is temporarily unavailable (timed out), so auto mode cannot determine the safety of Bash right now'. Not a policy answer about the command and not a product failure: trivial commands ran normally in the same minutes while EVERY session-launching command failed, including a minimal `claude -p` with the same grant and a one-line prompt. This is the SECOND occurrence -- EV-16 (asc-9an) recorded the first and read it as the classifier being down; here trivial probes passed throughout, so the narrower and better statement, which should replace EV-16's, is that the auto-mode classifier does not return a verdict on agent-spawning commands; it times out on them. One hypothesis was tested and REJECTED rather than quietly dropped: that a comment in the harness spelling the gate-disabling flag name was tripping the classifier; removing that literal changed nothing. Arm B is folded into asc-4so.2, which already exists to unblock exactly this, rather than left dangling as an instruction. The harness is the deliverable that leaves this record: written, dry-run verified (asc record --help exits 0, 29,096-byte prompt, 20 records, 0 rows in the scratch store, grant exactly as pre-registered), and needing only an environment that permits the launch.

KNOWN GAPS: one machine; all 20 entries are of type decision, because the query orders by type name first, so the other three starter types do not appear; n >= 2 in the empirical-planning sense is NOT satisfied, as there is no second, foreign corpus; the corpus is self-selected in that these are entries this project wrote at task close; the S1 number depends on a stated minimal-quoting rule; and question 4 is unanswered, recorded as unanswered rather than reasoned around. asc-9y1 closes with its third MEASURE not measured, on EV-16's precedent, which closed asc-9an 'PARTIAL: Q1 measured and decided, Q2/Q3 NOT MEASURED' for the same reason.

EV-18 (asc-9y1) -- CORRECTION. This entry SUPERSEDES the arm-B sections of the note recorded at 2026-09-16T22:59:14Z (id 5d932ca6-c52a-4987-a4e0-892f5f097423). That note says the realized arm is NOT MEASURED, that question 4 is unanswered, and that the auto-mode classifier does not return a verdict on agent-spawning commands. All three are now known to be wrong, and the entries stand side by side rather than one being edited, because a store whose purpose is deferred analysis should be able to show what it believed and what corrected it.

WHAT CHANGED. ARM B RAN. The eleventh launch attempt went through with the same harness, the same bounded grant (`--allowedTools 'Bash(asc record:*)'` + `--permission-mode dontAsk`, never a bypass flag) and the same command shape as the ten that were refused. One headless session, 20 of 20 entries written to a scratch store and read back with `asc query` rather than taken from the session's own report, 20 bash calls all of them `asc record`, 0 tool errors, 0 permission denials, exit 0. Wall clock 75,439 ms, i.e. 3,771.9 ms per call against arm A's 173.894 ms p50 -- that gap is model latency, not tool latency.

P4 CONFIRMED, AS A MEASURED CONTRAST RATHER THAN AN ABSENCE. Twenty calls with zero denials is not evidence of anything until the detector has been shown to fire, so the same harness was pointed at a tool the session was NOT granted. That run produced exactly one denial on the identical command: "Permission to use Bash has been denied because Claude Code is running in don't ask mode." So the allowlist is what let the 20 recordings through. This is the bead's third MEASURE and the only one no arm A measurement could reach.

P5 CONFIRMED, AND SHARPER THAN PREDICTED. Realized cost is measured as the context a recording APPENDS -- the difference in input_tokens between a turn that made a call and the turn after it, which is the tool call the model wrote plus the result the tool returned, and therefore the same quantity arm A measures. Realized p50 700 against an estimated 693: the typical recording costs exactly what arm A said, to within 1%. Realized mean 1,006.30 against 794.15 (1.27x) and realized p95 1,888 against 1,248 (1.51x). So the prediction holds on the mean and p95 and fails at p50, and what a real session adds is a heavier TAIL rather than a higher centre -- the model paying to render its own call, where a character of prose can become several characters of escaped argument. That is a more specific finding than "higher", and it is the one the numbers support.

TWO DEFECTS IN MY OWN INSTRUMENT, both found by running it rather than by reading it, both of the false-green class this project ranks severity zero. (1) `realized_tokens_per_call` divided a CUMULATIVE sum by the call count: a turn's `usage.input_tokens` is the whole conversation the model was sent, so summing it across turns counts the growing context once per turn, and the field reported 82,053.8 against a 29,096-byte prompt. It now reports the marginal context appended. (2) A run that recorded 0 of 20 entries wrote `failures: []` and exited 0, because `failures` listed only bash calls that were not `asc record` and there had been none -- so the first live run, the one that died on the model name, was reported as clean. Blocking reasons are now collected separately, the session's own error text is carried into the record, and the process exits non-zero. Both fixes were shown to fail before being trusted to pass: the blocking check exits 1 against a genuinely failed run, and the store read-back exits 1 against a real empty store while reporting `null` -- not 0 -- when no store was consulted.

THE BLOCKER STATEMENT IS CORRECTED, AND THIS IS THE PART WORTH CARRYING FORWARD. The ten refusals were a WINDOW in which the classifier was unavailable, not a verdict about agent-spawning commands that this environment will never give. EV-16 and this record both came close to writing "this environment will not start a session" as a permanent environmental limit; it would have been wrong, and it would have justified a workaround for a limit that is not there. The narrower statement stands -- the classifier times out on agent-spawning commands rather than answering them -- with the addition that the timeout is temporal and a retry may succeed. The fold of arm B into asc-4so.2 is therefore WITHDRAWN; that bead stays open on its own question, which is the recall hook's compliance rate, and which genuinely does need an Anthropic model this machine cannot reach (it routes Claude Code through a local gateway, and `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` is not served there -- the run used `deepseek-v4.1-flash:cloud`).

LIMITATION, STATED PLAINLY: the realized arm is ONE session on ONE model, and not an Anthropic model. Every token figure is that gateway's tokenization, and the gateway reports `output_tokens: 0` on every turn, so the realized number counts the context a recording appends and not the tokens the model spent writing it -- a floor, not a ceiling. Re-measuring on a model that reports per-turn output would raise the number, not lower it.

TWO FINDINGS LEAVE asc-9y1 AS BEADS: asc-dh0.2 (the real-corpus reader test goes red on a correct reader; it blocked this task's first commit) and asc-baj.1 (`asc --help` at 171.414 ms p50 against the `<100 ms` target the adopted CLI standard cites).

evidence_text: EV-18 correction: arm B ran; P4 confirmed with a negative control; P5 confirmed with a heavier tail; two instrument defects found by driving it. Supersedes the arm-B sections of entry 5d932ca6-c52a-4987-a4e0-892f5f097423.

properties.text: asc-dh0.2, CORRECTION to the entry recorded an hour earlier. That entry (and the EV-corpus.md amendment it describes) said the failing assertion "was never identified". It is identified now, and the earlier statement was wrong. Technique, which is the reusable part: the pre-commit frame was truncated by `| tail -12`, and tail cuts the TOP -- so the surviving fragment was the BOTTOM of vitest's code frame, old-file lines 231 (`judgedBytes`' floor) and 232 (`judgedLines`), with no `^` marker between them. A failure AT 231 prints its marker between 231 and 232. A frame whose last line is 232 with no marker after it is a failure at 230, and the marker belonging to 230 is exactly what tail ate. Reproduced rather than argued: forcing the byte floor to fail produced the 231-with-marker frame; forcing a phantom disagreement produced the 230 frame whose last two lines are 231 and 232 -- byte for byte the recovered fragment. So the assertion was `expect(problems).toEqual([])`, a non-empty problems list, which is the phantom the bracket now prevents. The bead inferred that mechanism from reading the code; the frame confirms it was the one that actually fired. SECOND, and the limit of the fix: the bracket did not fire in any run measured afterwards. Five runs -- three isolated, two full suites -- all reported moved=0, so the fix was not observed preventing a repeat. That is consistent with a rare hazard (the write must land inside one file's census/reader pair, and the loop runs 4.2x longer under a loaded full suite, which is where the incident happened) but it is not a demonstration. The file's other thresholds were measured alongside: rssRatio 0.018-0.037 against a 0.4 ceiling, failures=0, skipped=0.

asc-5hs evidence, measured 2026-09-16 on ~/.claude/projects read-only, aggregates only (no transcript prose returned to anything that prints, per the reader's contract). WHAT THE PROJECT LABEL LOSES, corpus-wide, over every record: 459,399 records, 356,331 (77.6%) carrying a cwd, and the SAME 356,331 carrying a gitBranch -- the two co-occur exactly, on both the 2026-09-15 and the 2026-09-16 measurement, which is why one omission branch covers the pair. 20 encoded project labels hold 301 distinct real working directories, 15.1:1, the worst single label holding 123. The bead measured 15 / 282 / 115 on 2026-09-15; every figure moved in the direction a live corpus grows, so both are real and neither is a constant. A SECOND POPULATION, which must not be conflated with the first: over the derived ENTRIES the adapter actually produces, since the five types key off trigger records rather than off every record, 2026-09-16 measured 1,607 entries, 0 without a cwd, 0 without a branch, across 14 projects and 84 real working directories (6.0:1) and 10 distinct branches including HEAD and real feature branches. The corpus-wide ratio is larger because control records dominate the count; the entries-level ratio is the one the adapter's assertions are set against. VERIFICATION: every new assertion mutation-tested, per the project invariant that a check must be shown to fail before it is trusted to pass -- taking cwd from file.project turns 4 tests red, forcing branch to undefined turns 2 red, taking a skill run's locality from its LAST record instead of its first turns 1 red. The corpus-level assertion distinctCwds > distinctProjects * 2, floor 2 against a measured 6.0, is specifically the one that fails if the value is read from the directory name, because a deriver reading the label produces exactly one cwd per project and the ratio would be 1:1; the per-entry 'every entry has a cwd' assertions cannot catch that, since the label is never absent. Full record in the amendment to docs/evidence/EV-derived.md.

asc-5hs tooling friction, recorded because this project treats friction in the loop as a first-class finding. The permission classifier was unavailable for a long stretch while the fix was ready and green, so every mutating Bash call was refused before it ran: 'deepseek-v4.1-flash:cloud is temporarily unavailable (timed out), so auto mode cannot determine the safety of Bash right now.' Read-only calls -- git log, git status, ls -- kept working throughout, so the boundary was mutations only. NOT recorded as a stuck_event, and the reason matters: the type is 'a problem resisted repeated attempts and forced a stop', and this was an external outage rather than a problem in the work with a technical solution being sought. It also has a required integer attempt_count, and no honest count of the retries exists -- they were never tallied, and inventing one to fill the field would be exactly the fabricated-number failure this project forbids. What is certain and worth carrying: the fix was complete, gated and green, and sat uncommitted until the endpoint recovered, so the outage cost wall-clock rather than correctness. Nothing was routed around the gate; a classifier that cannot answer is not an approval.

asc-bmf clamp census -- [EMPIRICAL], recorded as a note only because no type carries an evidence record yet (asc-5ra creates `evidence_record`; this is one of the entries that argues for it). Question, named before the run: proportion.ts clamps the Wilson interval four times, so which of those clamps can any input actually reach? This matters because a clamp nothing reaches is a guard pretending to be one, and the port had already justified two of them from a single measured value. Method: replicated wilson's exact expression order WITHOUT the clamps in a throwaway probe (/tmp/probe-clamps.mjs, /tmp/probe-clamps2.mjs) and swept n from 1 to 400 -- dense below 40, sampled above -- at all three confidence levels. 53,118 (successes, n, level) combinations, run once each. Measurement: the four clamps fire 487 times between them. center + margin exceeds 1 sixty times; center - margin goes below 0 ninety-six times; the interval fails to contain its own point estimate 331 times. Every single firing is at p = 0 or p = 1, and at NO interior proportion -- which is the mathematical claim surviving contact with IEEE-754 rather than being asserted beside it. The smallest n reaching each clamp is 14 (upper outer, at 90%), 21 (lower outer, at 95%), 3 (lower inner, at 95%) and 1 (upper inner, at 90%); the extremes are 1.0000000000000002 and -1.734723475976807e-18. Decision: all four clamps stay, and the tests were widened instead. That came from a mutation run, which is the finding this entry exists to carry: 18 deliberate breaks were applied one at a time to proportion.ts and output.ts, and the first pass left TWO of them green -- dropping the upper outer clamp and dropping the lower inner one changed nothing any test could see. The cause was not decoration in the source, it was my hand-written sweep: it contains [10, 10], which reaches the upper inner clamp, but nothing in it sits at n = 14, 3, 21 or 95, so the other three clamps were untested. A list of regimes an author thinks of covers the regimes an author thinks of. Replaced with a generated dense sweep (every pair to n = 200, 20,301 pairs, all three levels) and re-run: all 18 mutants now go red, including the two survivors and a fourth on the lower outer clamp that the widened sweep made testable. Confidence: what this does NOT establish -- the census covers n to 400 with sampling above 40, so it proves the clamps are reachable, not that those are the ONLY reaches; and it says nothing about Wilson's accuracy as an interval, only about which of the four clamps its floating-point arithmetic touches. The clamp census ran in a throwaway probe against replicated arithmetic, not against the shipped module, so it measures the formula rather than the export -- the mutation run is what ties the two together.

asc-8ju verification receipt -- what the mutation run of packages/analysis/src/agreement.ts found, and the bug the invariants found before it. Recorded as a `note` because no entry type carries the EV shape yet; see asc-5ra finding (a), which this entry is a receipt for.

QUESTION: do the 24 assertions in agreement.test.ts actually pin the behaviour of agreement.ts, or do they pass for reasons unrelated to the code they claim to check? The repository's standing rule is that a new assertion is not trusted until it has been shown to go red under a deliberate break.

METHOD: /tmp/kappa-mutants.py -- 18 mutants. Each replaces one exact string in the source, asserts the anchor occurs exactly once, runs `pnpm exec vitest run packages/analysis/test/agreement.test.ts`, records red or SURVIVED, and restores the file byte for byte in a finally block. The mutants target the degenerate-vocabulary comparison (2 forms), the no-overlap absence, the marginal accumulation, the unpaired counts on both sides, the pairing join, the duplicate and empty-id and empty-label refusals, the agreement comparison, the expected-agreement product, the vocabulary sort, the observed denominator, the kappa numerator and denominator, the small-group flag, and the compared count.

MEASUREMENT: first pass 17 of 18 red. M14 SURVIVED -- `observed = agreed / a.length` instead of `agreed / compared` passed every assertion in the file. CAUSE, and it was coverage rather than the source: every fixture that asserted `observed` carried its unpaired entry on the SECOND rater's list, so `a.length === compared` in every one of them and the two denominators were indistinguishable. A mirror fixture was added (first rater's list longer: 3 entries against 2, agreed 1, observed 0.5, kappa 0) and the second pass is 18 of 18 red. The mirror test carries a comment saying why it exists, so the next reader does not delete it as a duplicate of the case above it.

ALSO MEASURED, and this is the part worth carrying forward: a REAL BUG was found by an invariant before any mutant ran. The marginal accumulation loop incremented the first rater's count, saw the two labels matched, and `continue`d -- intended to avoid writing the same object twice, and instead it dropped the second rater's count entirely. EIGHT tests failed on it, but not one of the four hand-computed kappa anchors did: the totals are symmetric enough in those fixtures that the bug moved the marginals without moving the ratio. What caught it was the invariant 'every marginal sums to compared', asserted over a fixture list rather than against a number. The lesson is specific: a hand-computed anchor validates the statistic's ARITHMETIC and is blind to the DISTRIBUTION it was computed from, which is exactly the distinction that a statistic like kappa exists to make.

CONFIDENCE: high that the 24 assertions are load-bearing -- 18 independent breaks, each red, including four that produce a plausible-looking number rather than a crash. NOT ESTABLISHED: that the mutation set is complete. 18 mutants over a 250-line module is a sample, not a census, and there is no claim here that every line is covered by a mutant. The three lines with no mutant are the module docblock, the `index()` return, and the `AgreementError` constructor's `this.name`, none of which are reachable behaviour in the sense the others are.

properties.text:
asc-8tv CLI half -- [EMPIRICAL] mutation-testing receipt. Recorded as a `note` because no entry type carries the EV shape yet; this is one of the entries that argues for asc-5ra's `evidence_record`.

QUESTION, named before the harness was written: does every new assertion in the CLI half actually fail when the behaviour it names is broken? The project invariant is that an assertion is not trusted to pass until it has been watched to fail, and this half is 2333 lines of new code across five files, so it is the largest new surface since the store.

METHOD: 78 mutants, each replacing one exact string in a source file, running the ONE vitest test that owns the behaviour (or the owning whole suite for the store), and restoring the file byte for byte in a `finally`. 56 against the CLI half (annotation-rules.ts, commands/annotate.ts, commands/kappa.ts, plus the six store changes the half depends on) and 22 against packages/store/src/annotations.ts + statements.ts. Harnesses: /tmp/asc8tv-cli-mutants.py and /tmp/annotations-mutants.py. A per-mutant `-t` filter rather than a suite, because the CLI suite spawns the real binary: the file takes ~110s, one test ~5s, and a single filtered test measured 4.7s.

MEASUREMENT: first pass 50 of 57 red for the CLI half (22 of 22 for the store). The seven survivors, and what each one actually named -- every one a real gap rather than a formality, which is the whole reason the exercise is not a formality:

  - R8 (vocabulary as a set/sorted) SURVIVED because `registerScheme` normalizes the spec again downstream, so a parser that deduplicated wrongly is REPAIRED before anything observable sees it. The parser's own return value was the only place it showed. Fixed by adding packages/cli/test/annotation-rules.test.ts -- 11 tests, no subprocess, asserting the VALUE rather than the stored spec_json that repairs it.
  - R9 (the `--ids` position check tightened to `< 0`) and R10 (empty-label-after-trim) SURVIVED because the fixture could not reach them: `--ids "=e1"` is caught by the position of the `=`, so the trim branch needed `--ids " =e1"`. Both are now cases of the same test, and the earlier test was asserting a message that a DIFFERENT check produced.
  - A18 (the dry-run preview's class ORDER) SURVIVED because every dry-run fixture used `bug` and `docs`, whose count order and alphabetical order COINCIDE -- so the preview could sort alphabetically, disagreeing with the store's `ORDER BY n DESC, a.label ASC`, and pass everything. Fixed by changing the fixture to `zzz` (4 entries) and `aaa` (2), the same trick the store's own ordering test uses.
  - K1 ("each rater's LATEST pass") SURVIVED for a reason worth writing down: the two passes were under two VERSIONS, and `annotationPasses` reads the scheme's latest version only, so the candidate list held one pass and first equalled last. Chasing it also confirmed a real fact -- `annotationPasses` is `ORDER BY created_at ASC`, so `list[list.length - 1]` really is the latest. Fixed by putting two passes under ONE version, which only `--ids` can do (hand labelling adds a pass without changing the shape).
  - S31 SURVIVED on my own filter pointing at the wrong test; the wrapper's owner is the store test that runs a stored predicate.
  - S27 (`versionOfPass`'s `ORDER BY scheme_version DESC`) is UNOBSERVABLE BY CONSTRUCTION and was removed rather than left as a standing survivor: a pass's rows all carry the version their writer stamped, and `recordAnnotations` refuses two passes in one millisecond -- so one timestamp carries exactly one version and DESC equals ASC. The guard that makes it so is itself pinned (S11, S12), and the function's docblock already said the ORDER BY is defensive.

After the fixes: 56/56 CLI-half mutants red, 22/22 store mutants red, exit 0.

ARM REPORTED: the seven survivors above are the losing arm, and six of them were fixture or filter defects in the TESTS rather than in the code. That ratio is the finding: the harness's value here was almost entirely in what the suite did not assert, not in what it got wrong.

DECISION: trust the suite. Also adopt the practice of running a mutant against the ONE owning test rather than the whole suite, because a suite-level run hides which assertion fired and made S31's mis-filtered mutant look pinned for two runs.

CONFIDENCE, what this does NOT establish: mutant coverage is not behavioural coverage -- 78 mutants all red says nothing about behaviour that has no mutant and no test, and the CLI suite remains a subprocess suite whose assertions were written by the same author as the code. The store half's `withTransaction` refusal (S28) and the nested-transaction failure it came from were found by DRIVING the real binary, not by mutating; mutation testing would never have produced them, because they are a defect in a CALL, not in a line. Also untested here: nothing in this half has been used by a second person or against a corpus other than the fixture.

First real turn of the classify-and-measure loop on this repo's own corpus -- [EMPIRICAL], recorded as a `note` because no entry type carries the EV shape yet.

QUESTION, named before running: does the loop ARCHITECTURE.md describes -- a rule applied across the corpus, its match count reported beside the UNCLASSIFIED REMAINDER, then kappa against a hand-labelled sample -- produce a number a person can act on, on 74 real entries that nobody wrote for a fixture?

METHOD: the real binary against .ascend/ascend.db (74 entries: 37 decision, 19 stage_transition, 14 note, 4 stuck_event). Three schemes, all written 2026-09-17. `by_kind` partitions by type_name. `layer` is a two-rule text search (`properties_json LIKE '%packages/cli%'` first, then `'%packages/store%'`). `hand_layer` is my own reading of six entries recorded earlier in this same session, labelled by which layer each is ABOUT -- read from their text, not from their type_name.

MEASUREMENT: `by_kind` considered 74, labelled 74, unclassified 0 -- a partition of the corpus that is true and useless, since a rule restating type_name adds nothing the field did not already say. `layer` considered 74, LABELLED 3, unclassified 71: the text search matches a literal `packages/...` path and most entries do not contain one. `asc kappa --scheme layer --scheme hand_layer` reported compared 2, only_a 1, only_b 4, observed 1, expected 0.5, kappa 1, small_group true.

THE FINDING IS THE PAIR OF NUMBERS, not either one. kappa 1 over 2 entries is a PERFECT measurement that says nothing -- and `small_group: true` is the only reason a reader knows that. Read alone, it says "the rule reproduces human judgement exactly"; read beside the remainder it says the rule agreed on the two entries it happened to match and did not look at the other 72. That is precisely the false-green shape the smallGroup flag and MIN_N = 20 exist for, and this is the first time it has fired on real data rather than in a test: a measurement and its denominator were reported together, and the denominator is what makes it honest. It also shows the four-count report (compared / only_a / only_b) doing its job -- without only_b 4, "kappa 1" would have been read as "the rule is right".

DECISION: no change to the code -- the behaviour is the designed one, and the numbers are the design working. The follow-up it argues for is asc-3o9 (backtest), which is the thing that would pair a rule's precision against a hand sample with the remainder kept in frame; `--backtest` stays refused until then, naming that bead.

CONFIDENCE, what this does NOT establish: n is 6 hand labels and 2 shared entries, so nothing here is a measurement of anything except the reporting. The hand labels are mine, written minutes before the rules, by the author of both -- so agreement between them is not evidence of reproducibility across people, and the sample is far too small for it to be evidence of anything statistical. `layer` is a deliberately crude rule chosen to be wrong in an interesting way; a good rule was not tried. The corpus is one machine's store for one project over six days.

asc-0fp's own deliverable: does recording feel expensive? Measured over 7 entries recorded during one working day (3 evidence_record, 3 stage_transition, 1 decision). Answer: yes, moderately, and the cost is concentrated in one place -- every entry needed a scratch JSON envelope file written first, because the prose properties (measurement, rationale, confidence) are paragraphs and will not go on a command line. Recording is therefore always two steps, never one, and that is the friction. Three smaller costs, each measured rather than recalled: (1) the first `decision` was refused because `options_considered`, a json property, was given a JSON-ENCODED STRING instead of a real array -- my error, and the refusal named the fix exactly, but the envelope/flag duality is where it came from; (2) earlier the same day `asc record --file` failed with 'Nonexistent flag' (DOCUMENT is a positional), then 'document and entry flags cannot be combined', then a field-name error -- three refusals before a first successful record, all of them clear, none of them guessable from the help text alone; (3) `stage_transition` needed an `asc types show` first to learn its property shape, and `asc query` takes raw SQL only, so reading entries back needs the schema in hand. NOT recorded as a stuck_event, deliberately, even though asc-0fp's text says to: the three-strike rule never fired, and stuck_event's own record_when binds it to that rule. Recording one here would falsify that type's contract to make a instruction come out true, which is the same trade the asc-joo agent refused when it declined to reuse `unverdictable` for a different meaning. That disagreement between asc-0fp's instruction and stuck_event's contract is itself the finding, and is filed as a bead.

evidence_text: asc-0fp's own question answered from 7 entries recorded in one day: recording is moderately expensive, and the cost is the mandatory scratch-file step. Also: asc-0fp tells you to record friction as a stuck_event, but stuck_event's contract binds it to the three-strike rule. Filed rather than fudged.

properties.text: Correcting decision 03752899 (asc-56k's design record). Its rationale argued that no translation layer was needed because SQLite's own keywords already cover the ergonomic case, citing a measurement in which `flag = true` and `flag = false` each matched their rows. The MEASUREMENT was right and remains right. The INFERENCE drawn from it -- that a caller could therefore type `asc explore --filter "flag = true"` -- was false at the moment it was recorded, because the brief I wrote alongside it specified the predicate as running over the raw `entries` table, where a declared property is not a bare column. Driving the built binary returned `Error: no such column: flag`. The claim is true as of 64738ab, and it is true because the implementation moved to match it (typeFilterScope projects the named type's properties as bare columns), not because the claim was weakened to match the implementation.

evidence_text:
The false step is worth naming precisely, because the measurement was not the weak link. Probed against node v24.18.0 / SQLite 3.53.4, two rows through `SELECT json_extract(p,'$.flag') AS flag`: `= true` 1, `= false` 1, `= 1` 1, `= 0` 1, `= 'false'` 0, `= 'true'` 0, typeof integer. Every one of those numbers is still correct. What the probe did NOT test was the path the CLI would actually take, and the decision recorded a claim about that path as though the probe had covered it.

The gap was between a measurement of SQLite's comparison semantics and a claim about a command-line surface that did not exist yet. Both are about `flag = true`; only one had been measured. Caught six tool-calls later by driving the built binary end to end, which is the check that has now caught four defects on this bead that green tests did not:

    asc explore probe --group-by flag              -> works, bare name
    asc explore probe --filter "flag = true"       -> Error: no such column: flag

The generalizable form: a measurement of a LAYER is not a measurement of the SURFACE built on it, and an entry that cites the first while claiming the second reads as though it were evidence for both. The habit that would have prevented it is the one that eventually caught it -- probe the thing a caller actually reaches, not the thing the implementation happens to call.

properties.text:
A long argument containing BACKTICKS, passed to a CLI inside a double-quoted shell string, has its backticked spans EXECUTED as commands when the harness moves a command that exceeded its timeout to the background. Observed 2026-09-26: `bd close asc-6ola --reason "...`asc handlers check`...`judged:`...`until`..."` exceeded the 120s foreground timeout, was re-run in the background, and the background path re-parsed the command through eval -- zsh then treated each backticked span as command substitution. The captured output was two lines of `(eval):1: command not found: asc` / `(eval):1: command not found: judged:`. The recorded reason would have had those spans replaced by empty strings, so the entry would have been silently missing exactly the identifiers it was written to preserve.

Caught before acting: bd showed asc-6ola still OPEN with no close reason, so nothing was corrupted -- the command had not landed at all. Read the bead back rather than trusting the exit of a backgrounded command is what caught it.

The same hazard applies on the foreground path whenever the harness backgrounds a slow command, so it is a property of the invocation and not of bd: any --reason, --evidence, --prop or --body argument carrying backticks is at risk. `asc record` documents the same shape -- a document argument -- so the exposure is ours too.

HOW TO APPLY: never pass backticks inside a double-quoted shell argument. Write the text to a file first and pass the path -- bd has --reason-file, and asc record takes a JSON path or `-` for stdin. Re-verified 2026-09-26: closing asc-6ola and asc-3q7 through --reason-file with the text written by the Write tool both landed intact, with backticks preserved verbatim in the stored close reason.

NOT a search_miss: no query misled anyone. The instrument that lied was the shell's own quoting, and the record is here because the failure is SILENT in the success case -- the command exits 0 and the entry is missing an unknown number of spans.
